opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I'd call it a pretty typical piece of early-career computer vision work: very much a product of its time. Back then the field was still dominated by hand-crafted features and carefully engineered pipelines. You'd pick some descriptor, design a clever way to pool or encode it, tune things on a benchmark, and if you got a few points of improvement, that was a paper.

So in terms of the craft, I think it taught me a lot: how to set up experiments, how to read the literature, how to write. But in terms of lasting scientific contribution, I'd be honest and say it was incremental. It wasn't the kind of work that changes how people think about the problem. And within a few years, deep learning came along and basically swept that whole style of research away. A lot of the tricks we cared about just stopped mattering once you could learn the representation end to end.

That experience actually shaped how I think about research now. It made me ask: is this work going to survive the next paradigm shift, or is it just squeezing a benchmark? I'd much rather work on something that's about representations, about what the right inductive biases are, about questions that stay meaningful even when the tools change. So I don't regret that paper. It was a necessary step. But I see it more as training than as the work that defines me.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd call it a student paper more than anything else. It came from very early in my research life, before I had a real sense of taste for what problems mattered. Face recognition at the time was one of those well-trodden benchmarks where you could learn the whole pipeline of vision research: collect data, design features, train a classifier, tune it, write it up. So that's what it was for me, a way to learn the craft.

I don't think it was an important piece of work scientifically. It was incremental, and it lived inside a paradigm that was about to be swept away by deep learning. If you read it today, you'd see the hand-designed features, the careful engineering around alignment and lighting, all the things that the field spent years perfecting and then discovered a network could just learn end to end.

But I also don't look down on it. Doing that kind of work taught me how fragile a lot of the "clever" tricks were, and how much of the gain came from data and representation rather than from the specific model. That instinct carried into everything I did later, from HED and ResNeXt to the self-supervised and generative work. So I'd characterize it as a necessary but forgettable paper. It mattered for the person who wrote it, not for the field.

astra-6.text: I’d characterize it as an early, fairly task-specific computer-vision paper. We were focused on a concrete problem—face recognition—and trying to design a method that worked well for it. I wouldn’t frame it as a broad statement about visual intelligence. For me, it was also a way to learn how to do research: turn an idea into experiments, see what the results actually support, and understand the limitations.
